blocks.text: Your Personal Profile
Before You Begin
What you are completing is your TMG180 Personal Profile.
Before we explain why it can be useful, we want to acknowledge something important.
Being asked questions about your life can feel invasive.

Forms, assessments, reviews and requests for evidence can ask very personal questions about your body, your health, your relationships, your home, things you find difficult, and experiences you may not usually discuss with other people.
For some people this is straightforward. For others it can feel uncomfortable, exhausting or overwhelming.

Some people have also had previous experiences with child protection, out-of-home care, state guardianship, mental-health services, hospitals, justice systems, homelessness services, disability services or other systems where information was collected about them.
Those experiences may have involved feeling controlled, judged, moved, disbelieved, assessed, recorded or spoken about rather than listened to.
PERSONAL PROFILE TRIAL DRAFT V4 copy copy.docx
For some people, being asked similar questions again can bring back memories, distress or feelings associated with those experiences.
You remain in control of how you complete this Profile.
You can complete it by yourself.
You can ask someone you trust to help you.
You can complete one section and come back later.
You can pause.
You can skip questions.
You can say that something does not apply to you.
You can say you don’t know.
You can change an answer later.
And you can explain something completely differently in your own words.
You do not have to tell your whole life story to complete your Personal Profile.
The purpose is to help you describe what is relevant to understanding you, your everyday life and the support you need.
Understanding your everyday life, in your own words
Why this is important

The NDIS is not based simply on the name of your diagnosis. The NDIS Act and current NDIS framework consider your impairment, your functional capacity and how your impairment affects your everyday life.
This means that understanding and being able to explain what your disability means for you is important.
Two people can have the same diagnosis and experience very different strengths, difficulties and support needs. Some impairments are easy for other people to see. Others are not.
You may also be able to do something sometimes, or have the physical ability and knowledge to do it, but still have difficulty:
getting started;
planning, organising or remembering what needs to happen;
processing information or following several steps;
doing something safely;
managing pain, fatigue, anxiety, panic, sensory demands or other symptoms;
doing something reliably and consistently;
repeating it as often as everyday life requires;
doing it without significant physical, mental or emotional effort or recovery; or
having enough capacity left afterwards for other necessary activities and the things that matter to you.
Being able to complete a task does not always tell the whole story about how your impairment affects your everyday life.
Helping you understand your own functional needs
Words such as impairment, functional capacity, executive functioning, sensory processing, regulation, and support needs can sound complicated.
But they often describe very ordinary things that happen in everyday life.
This Personal Profile explains different areas of functioning in everyday language. Each section provides examples and prompts to help you think about your own experience.
The prompts are not answers we want you to give.

They are there because it can be difficult to recognise or put into words something you have experienced for a long time. They may help you identify something that applies to you — or help you recognise that it doesn’t.
You can say:

Yes.
Yes, with support or adjustments.
Sometimes.
No.
I’m not sure.
I haven’t tried this.
And importantly, you can explain why.
Every section also gives you space to describe what happens in your own words.
There are no answers you are expected to give. The purpose is to make what is true for you easier to understand and communicate — without exaggerating your difficulties and without minimising them.
Your diagnosis is important — but it doesn’t tell your whole story
You can include any diagnoses, disabilities or health conditions you want people supporting you to understand.
For some people, having workers understand their diagnosis is important. For others, they may prefer to share only information relevant to the support being provided.
A diagnosis can help explain an impairment, but a diagnosis by itself cannot tell another person exactly how that impairment affects you.
Your Profile therefore records both where relevant:
what you want people to know about your disability or diagnosis
and
what actually happens in your everyday life.
You remain a person first — with strengths, preferences, relationships, goals, interests, abilities and things that matter to you.
Understanding the whole effect on your life
Everyday functioning isn’t only about whether you can shower, dress, prepare food, clean your home or leave the house.

Physical functioning, executive functioning, cognition, communication, sensory experiences, pain, fatigue, anxiety, panic, emotional regulation, nutrition, movement, relationships, your environment and many other things can interact.
Sometimes you can complete the necessary things in life, but doing them takes so much physical, cognitive or emotional effort that there is little capacity left for anything else.
You may have to choose between necessary activities.
You may need significant recovery afterwards.
You may have little capacity remaining for relationships, physical activity, interests, community participation or things you enjoy.
That impact is also part of understanding your everyday life.
The Profile helps you describe not only whether something gets done, but what it takes for you to do it and what effect that has on the rest of your life.
What you already have and what you have already tried
Understanding support needs also means understanding what is already around you.
Your Profile can record the mainstream, community, health, allied-health, informal and disability supports you already use, as well as strategies, routines, equipment and other things that help you.
It can also record things you have already tried — including what worked, what partly worked, what didn’t work, what wasn’t suitable or accessible, and what you continue to use.
This helps create a more complete picture without assuming that the NDIS is the only source of support in your life.
Improvement and permanent or ongoing impairment can exist together
Treatment, strategies, learning, environmental changes and appropriate support can improve how someone functions.
That does not necessarily mean an underlying permanent or enduring impairment has disappeared.
Sometimes a person functions better because something is working.
Your Profile and later updates can help show:
what has improved; what helped; what support or structure remains necessary; what happens without it; and what impairment or functional difficulty continues over time.
This allows improvement to be recorded accurately without treating improvement itself as evidence that an enduring impairment no longer exists.
Building your own evidence over time

Your Personal Profile provides a baseline — a starting picture of your everyday functioning, strengths, difficulties, goals, existing supports, what you have tried, what helps and what remains difficult.
It then connects with your ongoing TMG records.
Your Daily Notes record what actually happened during support.
Your Monthly Summaries help identify patterns over time.
Your Profile Updates record meaningful changes, improvements, new difficulties, new strategies and things that remain the same.
TMG keeps this information connected for you.

As information builds over time, the platform can collate what has been recorded and create a summary or report for the period you choose — for example, three months, six months, your current plan period, or when you are preparing for a plan reassessment.
The report is based on the information that has actually been recorded. Its purpose is to help organise that information and make patterns over time easier to understand.
This means you don’t have to search through months of notes or try to remember everything at once.

When your NDIS plan is reviewed or reassessed, you can have an organised record to help you explain how your impairments affect your everyday life in your own words, alongside relevant professional assessments and other evidence.
Professional evidence and your own evidence can work together
Professional assessments, reports and clinical evidence can be important.
But you should also be able to understand and communicate your own everyday experience.
Your Profile helps give you the language and structure to do that.
It means you do not have to rely only on another person interpreting your life for you.
The information you provide, the support that actually occurs, your observations and choices, relevant worker observations and professional evidence can each contribute different information.
Together, they can create a clearer picture of what happens over time, rather than relying only on a snapshot from one appointment or assessment.
Helping workers understand you
You shouldn’t have to explain everything from the beginning every time somebody new supports you.
Your Profile can help the people you choose to work with understand relevant information before they begin — including:

what matters to you; your goals; what you prefer; what you can do independently; where you want assistance; what helps; what doesn’t help; and anything you want them to understand about working alongside you.
This can reduce guesswork for workers while giving you greater control over how you are understood and supported.
It does not mean every worker needs access to your entire Profile.
Different sections can be relevant to different people. You should only need to share information that is appropriate for the support being provided, unless you choose to share more.
Your Profile belongs to you
This Profile is designed to support your understanding, your voice, your choices and your autonomy.
It is not an assessment of your worth or a test you need to pass.
It does not decide what the NDIS will fund, and it does not replace professional evidence where professional evidence is required.
Instead, it helps you understand and record:

This is what I can do.
This is what is difficult for me.
This is what I have already tried.
This is what I already have around me.
This is what helps.
This is the support or adjustment I need.
This is what happens when I have that support.
This is what happens when I don’t.
This is what has improved.
This is what remains difficult.
This is the effect on the rest of my life.
And this is what I want you to understand about me.
You don’t need to complete everything at once.
You can work through the sections that are relevant to you, return to them when you need to, and update individual areas when something meaningfully changes.
The purpose is simple: to help make your actual everyday life understandable — to you and, when you choose, to the people supporting you.

blocks.text: Module 2 — About Me, My Disability and What Matters to Me
Before we start
This section helps build a picture of you as a whole person before we look more closely at different areas of everyday functioning.
Your disability or diagnosis may be an important part of your life, but it is not everything about you.

This section gives you space to record what you want people to understand about you, your disability or health conditions, your goals, the supports already around you, and things you have already tried.
You only need to share information that is relevant and that you choose to include.
1. About Me
A little about me
Everyone is different. Knowing something about you can help people understand how to work alongside you rather than making assumptions based only on your disability or diagnosis.
Name I like to be called:
Pronouns, if I want to include them:
Things that are important to me:
Things I enjoy or am interested in:
People, animals, relationships or communities that are important to me:
Things I am good at or strengths I want people to know about:
What helps me feel comfortable with people supporting me?
You might think about communication, humour, personality, privacy, personal space, being given time, being asked rather than told, predictability, flexibility or anything else that matters to you.
Prompts — choose anything that applies:

☐ I like people to ask before assisting me
☐ I prefer clear and direct communication
☐ I need extra time to process information
☐ I like to know what is happening beforehand
☐ I prefer flexibility rather than a rigid routine
☐ I prefer predictable routines
☐ Humour is important to me
☐ I prefer quieter interactions
☐ I like to do as much as I can for myself
☐ I want help offered without having to repeatedly ask
☐ I prefer people not to assume what I need
☐ Something else: __________________
In my own words — what would I like someone supporting me to understand about me?
2. My Disability, Diagnosis or Health Conditions
Why we ask
The NDIS considers the functional impact of impairment, rather than assuming that everyone with the same diagnosis has the same support needs.
However, your diagnosis or health condition can still be important information.
You may want the people supporting you to understand it. It may also help provide context for professional evidence and for understanding why particular functional difficulties occur.
Having a diagnosis does not automatically tell another person what you can or cannot do.
Later sections will help you describe what actually happens in your everyday life.
What would I like to record?
My primary disability, diagnosis or condition, if I want to include it:
Other diagnoses, disabilities or health conditions I want included:

☐ I prefer not to record my diagnosis here
☐ I have a diagnosis but don’t want all workers to see it
☐ I don’t currently have a diagnosis for some of the difficulties I experience
☐ I am still undergoing assessment
☐ Something else: __________________
What does this mean to me?
A medical description may not explain what living with a condition is actually like.
Is there anything you want people to understand about your disability, diagnosis or health condition?
Are there things you do NOT want people to assume because of your diagnosis?
That second question is important. A diagnostic label shouldn’t become a shortcut for workers to decide what somebody needs.
3. My Goals
Why goals matter
Your NDIS goals describe things you want to work towards, maintain or have greater opportunity to do in your life.
Sometimes formal goal wording doesn’t fully explain what a goal means to the person.
This section lets you record the goal and then explain what it actually means to you.
Goal
My NDIS goal:
What does this goal mean to me in everyday life?
Why is this important to me?
What parts of my everyday life are connected with this goal?

☐ Personal care
☐ Home and household life
☐ Physical health and movement
☐ Nutrition and meals
☐ Communication
☐ Executive functioning / organisation
☐ Emotional wellbeing or regulation
☐ Relationships and connection
☐ Community participation
☐ Work, education or learning
☐ Independence
☐ Maintaining my current abilities
☐ Something else: __________________
What already helps me work towards or maintain this goal?
What makes this difficult?
What support or adjustments help?
In my own words — what would progress with this goal look like for me?
+ Add another goal

That last question matters because progress doesn’t always mean becoming completely independent. Sometimes progress can mean maintaining capacity, preventing deterioration, doing something more reliably, needing less assistance, finding an effective adjustment, or having enough support to continue doing something important.
4. What I Already Have Around Me
Why we ask
Disability support does not exist separately from the rest of your life.
You may already receive help from family or friends, health professionals, community organisations, mainstream services, technology, routines or other supports.
Understanding what is already working helps build an accurate picture of your life.
It can also help distinguish between what is already available and effective, what needs adjustment, and where a need remains unmet.
People who support me informally
This might include family, friends, neighbours or other people you trust.
Who or what support do I have?
What do they help me with?
How often?
Is this support reliable and sustainable?

☐ Yes
☐ Mostly
☐ Sometimes
☐ No
☐ I’m not sure
Why? / Is there anything important about this support?
Health and allied-health supports
This could include your GP, specialist, psychologist, occupational therapist, physiotherapist, exercise physiologist, dietitian or other health professionals.
Support/service: __________________
What does this help with? __________________
Is it currently helping?

☐ Yes
☐ Yes, partly
☐ Sometimes
☐ No
☐ I’m not sure yet
Anything you want to explain:
Mainstream and community supports

These might include community organisations, recreation programs, neighbourhood services, transport, education, employment services, council programs, peer groups or other services available to the wider community.
What do I currently use?
Does it meet my needs?

☐ Yes
☐ Yes, with adjustments or support
☐ Sometimes
☐ No
☐ I’m not sure
Why?
If something works well, what makes it work?
If it only works with adjustments, what adjustments or assistance make it accessible?
If it works sometimes, what changes when it does or doesn’t work?
If it doesn’t work, what makes it difficult or inaccessible?
If you’re unsure, is that because you haven’t tried it, don’t have enough information, would need adjustments, or something else?
In my own words:
That follows the rule we established: a yes or no should not be interpreted without understanding why.
5. Things I Have Already Tried
Why this matters
People often try many different ways of managing an impairment or making everyday life easier.
Some work very well.
Some help partly.
Some work for a while.
Some don’t help.
Some are inaccessible or unsuitable.
And some things simply haven’t been tried.
Recording this helps avoid repeatedly starting from the assumption that nothing has previously been attempted.
What have I tried?
This might include:

☐ Medical treatment
☐ Medication
☐ Therapy or counselling
☐ Rehabilitation
☐ Allied health
☐ Exercise or physical activity approaches
☐ Nutrition or meal strategies
☐ Equipment or assistive technology
☐ Apps, reminders or organisational tools
☐ Routines or environmental changes
☐ Mainstream services
☐ Community/group programs
☐ Disability supports
☐ Informal/family support
☐ Something else: __________________
For each relevant item:
What did I try?
What was it intended to help with?
What happened?

☐ It helped significantly
☐ It helped partly
☐ It helped temporarily
☐ It didn’t help
☐ It made things more difficult
☐ It wasn’t suitable for me
☐ I couldn’t access it
☐ I stopped for another reason
☐ I’m still using it
☐ I’m not sure yet
Tell us why
What helped? What didn’t? What made it suitable or unsuitable?
Do you have supporting information about this if you choose to provide it?

☐ Yes
☐ No
☐ I’m not sure
And importantly:
Things I haven’t tried
There can be many reasons something hasn’t been tried.

☐ I haven’t known it was available
☐ It isn’t available where I live
☐ I couldn’t access it
☐ Cost was a barrier
☐ My disability made accessing it difficult
☐ I would need adjustments or assistance to try it
☐ It wasn’t recommended for me
☐ It wasn’t appropriate for me
☐ I chose not to pursue it
☐ I’m waiting to access it
☐ Other: __________________
In my own words:
We should not imply that someone must exhaust every conceivable treatment or community option.
6. What Helps Me Function
This is where we start connecting everything before entering the detailed functional modules.
Things that make everyday life easier for me

☐ Another person being present
☐ Prompting or reminders
☐ Appointments or external structure
☐ Written instructions or checklists
☐ Breaking tasks into smaller steps
☐ Extra processing time
☐ Familiar people
☐ Familiar environments
☐ Quiet or low-sensory environments
☐ Flexible timing
☐ Predictable routines
☐ Physical assistance
☐ Equipment or technology
☐ Rest and recovery periods
☐ Help organising or prioritising
☐ Emotional reassurance or encouragement
☐ Individual rather than group support
☐ Adjustments to an activity or environment
☐ Something else: __________________
Why do these things help me?
What tends to happen when the things that help me aren’t available?
In my own words — what helps me live my everyday life in a way that works for me?

blocks.text: Module 4 — My Body, Movement & Physical Abilities
Understanding your body and movement
Our bodies affect how we move through everyday life.
This can include things such as movement, strength, balance, coordination, stamina, flexibility, pain, fatigue, fine motor skills, physical safety and recovery.
Your physical abilities may be consistent, or they may change from day to day or during the same day.

You might also have the physical ability to do something but find it difficult to start, organise, continue or repeat because of fatigue, executive functioning, anxiety, panic, sensory overload, concentration or other effects of your disability or health.
This section looks at the whole picture.

It is not about testing how physically capable you are. It is about helping you describe what your body is like for you, what you can do, what can be difficult, what helps, and how this affects your everyday life.
What can my body do?
Let’s start with what you can do.
You may do these things independently, with an adjustment, with equipment, with another person’s assistance, sometimes, or not at all.
Moving around
How do you usually move around your home and community?

☐ I walk independently
☐ I walk with equipment or an aid
☐ I use a wheelchair or other mobility equipment
☐ I use different ways of getting around in different situations
☐ I need another person’s physical assistance
☐ I need someone nearby for safety or confidence
☐ I can move around but only for limited distances or periods
☐ My ability varies
☐ Something different for me: __________
Is there anything you’d like us to understand about how you move around?
Strength, balance and coordination
Do any of these apply to you?

☐ My strength generally meets my everyday needs
☐ I experience muscle weakness
☐ My strength varies
☐ I have difficulty with balance
☐ I am at risk of falling
☐ I have fallen or nearly fallen
☐ I have difficulty coordinating some movements
☐ I experience tremor or involuntary movement
☐ I have difficulty getting up or down
☐ Stairs are difficult
☐ Uneven surfaces are difficult
☐ Carrying things affects my balance or movement
☐ I need equipment, another person or something to hold onto

What does this look like in your everyday life?
What helps?
Using my hands and doing smaller movements
Physical ability isn’t only about walking.
Hands, fingers, grip and coordination can affect many ordinary activities.

☐ Holding or gripping objects

What happens for you?
Have you found ways of adapting how you do these things?
That last question should recur throughout the Profile. Adaptation is evidence of resourcefulness as well as information about functional need.

Pain can affect people very differently.

Energy, stamina and fatigue

What does fatigue feel like for you?

What happens when you exceed what your body can manage?
My body can be different at different times
Your answer does not have to describe every day as though it were the same.
Does your physical ability change depending on:

☐ Time of day
☐ Sleep
☐ Pain
☐ Fatigue
☐ Medication

☐ Stress

What is a more difficult day like?
How often do the more difficult periods occur?
This gives us the longitudinal anchor without turning it into scoring.
Sometimes the barrier isn’t purely physical
This section is important.
You may physically be able to perform an activity but still find it difficult to access or maintain it.
Do any of these affect your physical activities?

☐ Difficulty getting started
☐ Difficulty planning or organising the activity
☐ Forgetting

☐ Anxiety

☐ None of these significantly affect me
What actually happens for you?
What helps?
That’s where the whole-person model becomes real rather than merely being written in TMG philosophy.
Movement and physical activity
Why movement matters
Regular movement and physical activity can be important for maintaining physical and mental health.
Depending on the person and the activity, movement can support strength, mobility, balance, cardiovascular health, physical conditioning, sleep, mood, cognition and general health and wellbeing.
For someone living with disability, maintaining appropriate physical activity may also help maintain abilities and reduce the effects of inactivity or deconditioning.
But knowing that physical activity is beneficial doesn’t necessarily make it accessible.
Disability can affect what activity is safe, what is possible, where it can happen, whether someone can initiate and maintain it, and what assistance or expertise they need.
This section isn’t about whether somebody should receive funding for a gym membership.
It is about understanding your ability to access appropriate movement and physical activity and what, if anything, gets in the way.

In my own words:

That’s exactly the distinction we identified earlier: don’t turn preference into impairment, but don’t turn the existence of a community option into evidence that the person can actually use it either.
What do I need from someone supporting my physical activity?

What is executive functioning?
Executive functioning is a term used for some of the processes that help us turn thoughts and intentions into action.
We use these processes throughout everyday life — often without thinking about them — when we:
get started on something;
decide what needs doing first;
plan and organise;
remember what we are doing;
follow several steps;
manage time;
shift from one activity to another;
stay with something until it is finished; and
manage several demands without becoming overwhelmed.
Difficulties with executive functioning do not mean that you don’t understand what needs to be done, don’t care about doing it, or aren’t trying.
Sometimes a person can know exactly what needs to happen, want to do it and have the physical skills to do it, but still have difficulty turning that intention into action.
You may also be very capable once you have started.
That is why looking only at whether somebody can perform a task may not show the whole functional picture.

What does personal care mean?
Looking after ourselves involves many ordinary, personal things we do to care for our bodies and feel comfortable in everyday life.
This can include:
showering or bathing, washing, dressing, grooming, oral care, hair care, toileting, continence, skin care and other personal routines that matter to you.
For some people these things are straightforward.
For others, they may involve physical assistance, equipment, prompting, planning, pain, fatigue, sensory difficulties, anxiety, trauma responses, executive functioning or other barriers.
And sometimes a person can physically perform the task but cannot reliably initiate or maintain it as often as they need to.
Personal care is also private.

Module 7 — Getting Around & Leaving Home
Getting out and about can involve more than getting from one place to another
Leaving home can be simple for some people and involve many different steps for others.
It can include:

Some people are comfortable going out alone. Some prefer company. Some need another person because of their disability. Some can manage familiar places but not unfamiliar ones.

blocks.text: Module 8 — Food, Meals & Everyday Nutrition
Food is about more than cooking
Food is part of everyday life.
It can be about nutrition, health, enjoyment, culture, family, comfort, routine, celebration, connection and pleasure.
For some people, choosing, preparing and eating food is straightforward. For others, disability or health conditions can affect different parts of the process.
This might involve:
recognising hunger or thirst → deciding what to eat → planning → shopping → preparing food → cooking safely → eating and drinking → getting enough nutrition → cleaning up afterwards.

Physical ability, executive functioning, fatigue, pain, sensory experiences, appetite, emotions, swallowing, coordination, medication, anxiety, depression, trauma-related responses and other factors can all play a part.
You might love food and still struggle to eat enough.
You might be able to cook but struggle to start.
You might eat well sometimes and find it much harder at other times.
You might need another person’s assistance, specialist equipment or an individual mealtime management plan.
Or food and meals might not be an area where you need any support at all.
This section is about what food and eating are actually like for you.
What is food like for me?
Let’s start with the person, rather than the problem.

blocks.text: Module 9 — My Home & Everyday Household Tasks
My home is my space
Our homes are where much of everyday life happens.

Looking after a home can involve many different activities — cleaning, laundry, dishes, changing bedding, organising belongings, managing rubbish, keeping track of household supplies, noticing when something needs attention and, for some people, looking after an outdoor area.
People also have very different ideas about what makes a home comfortable.

Some people like everything organised and put away. Some prefer having things where they can see them. Some enjoy housework. Some don’t. Some are comfortable with a little clutter. Some find clutter overwhelming.
There isn’t one correct way your home should look.
This section is about whether your home works for you and whether disability or health-related difficulties affect your ability to keep it the way you want it.
What does a comfortable home mean to me?

blocks.text: Module 10 — Keeping My Mind & Body Healthy
Looking after health is part of everyday life
Living well isn’t only about completing everyday tasks.
Our bodies and minds need things that help us maintain health, abilities, wellbeing and everyday functioning over time.
Some of these things are important for health generally, such as appropriate physical activity, movement, nutrition, sleep and rest.
Others are individual. Over time, you may have discovered particular routines, activities, people, environments, therapies or strategies that help you remain well.
This section helps record both.
It isn’t a list of things you are expected to do, and completing it does not mean that every activity or support listed will necessarily be funded.

It helps build a clearer picture of what maintains your health and functioning, what you already use, what works, what you have tried, and whether disability-related barriers affect your ability to access it.
Movement & Physical Activity
Physical activity isn’t simply an optional extra
Appropriate physical activity and movement are important parts of maintaining physical and mental health.
They can contribute to things such as strength, mobility, balance, cardiovascular health, physical conditioning, bone and muscle health, sleep, mood and overall health and wellbeing.

For people living with disability or health conditions, appropriate movement may also be important for maintaining existing abilities, reducing deconditioning and supporting everyday physical capacity.
But physical activity doesn’t look the same for everybody.
It does not necessarily mean going to a gym, playing sport or exercising independently.
For one person it may be walking or strength training.
For another it may be swimming, adapted exercise, physiotherapy exercises or an individual exercise program.

For someone with significant physical limitations it may include supported or assisted movement, range-of-motion activities, stretching or positioning, where these have been recommended as appropriate for that person.
The question isn’t:
“Do you exercise enough?”
It is:
“What movement is appropriate for your body, what helps maintain your health and abilities, and can you actually access it?”

blocks.text: Module 11 — My Emotions, Stress & Nervous System
We all respond to stress differently
Our emotions and nervous system are part of how we respond to everyday life.
Stress can affect our body, thinking, emotions, communication, behaviour, energy and ability to do everyday things.
For some people these effects are relatively small.

For others, disability, health conditions, trauma, neurodivergence, chronic pain, sensory processing, anxiety, depression or other experiences can make these responses stronger, happen more often, last longer, or require more recovery.
Sometimes there is an obvious reason.
Sometimes there isn’t.
And sometimes other people see a person’s response without understanding what is happening underneath it.
This section isn’t about judging emotions as good or bad or deciding how you should respond.
It helps you describe:
what happens for you → what you notice → what other people might notice → what affects you → what helps → what makes things worse → how you want to be supported → what happens afterwards.

blocks.text: Module 12 — My Health, Medication & Ongoing Health Needs
My health is part of my everyday life
Everyone manages their health in different ways.

For some people, health care is relatively straightforward. For others, physical conditions, mental health conditions, chronic illness, pain, fatigue, medication, treatments or ongoing health needs can take significant time, energy, planning and support.
Health can also fluctuate.
A person may manage their health independently most of the time and need considerably more assistance during periods of illness, deterioration, pain, fatigue or emotional distress.
This section isn’t asking you to provide your entire medical history.
It’s about understanding:

what health needs you live with → how they affect everyday life → what treatment or management you already have → what you manage yourself → where you need assistance → what happens when your health changes.
My current health
Do you live with ongoing health conditions or health needs?

☐ Yes — physical health
☐ Yes — mental health

Some people don’t take medication. Others manage one medication easily. Some have complex medication routines.

And again, TMG records the established need and plan; it doesn’t clinically prescribe it.
Continence & Toileting-Related Health Needs

When One Thing Affects Everything Else

☐ Personal care

☐ Medication routines
☐ Household tasks
☐ Movement/physical activity
☐ Sleep
☐ Executive functioning

☐ Leaving home
☐ Appointments

What Already Works
Here it makes sense to ask this specifically about health management, rather than repeating it as a generic question in every functional module.

These could include medication routines, professionals, therapies, appointments, equipment, reminders, pacing strategies, treatment plans or things you’ve developed yourself.

☐ Help organising appointments

In My Own Words
You are more than your medical history.

This section isn’t asking you to list everything that has ever happened to your body or mind. It is here to help explain the health needs that affect your everyday life, how you currently manage them, what already works and where you need assistance.

Sometimes difficulty doesn’t sit entirely within a person’s body or mind.

The equipment we use, technology available to us, how our home is arranged, accessibility, noise, lighting, temperature, transport and the way information is presented can make everyday activities easier or much harder.
A person may be able to do something independently in one environment and need considerable assistance in another.
Equipment and technology can also allow someone to do something themselves that would otherwise require another person’s assistance.
This section helps describe:

Do you use communication equipment or technology?

☐ No
☐ AAC/communication device
☐ Communication app
☐ Speech-to-text
☐ Text-to-speech
☐ Hearing technology
☐ Visual communication
☐ Another communication method: __________
What should someone know about communicating accessibly with you?
Transport & Getting Where I Need to Go
We’ve already covered leaving home and getting around in Module 7, so we don’t need to repeat the functional assessment here.
Here we’re asking specifically whether transport and environmental accessibility affect access.
What transport do you currently use?

☐ Drive myself
☐ Family/friends
☐ Support worker
☐ Taxi/rideshare
☐ Public transport
☐ Community transport
☐ Accessible/specialised transport
☐ Walk/wheel
☐ Something else: __________
Does your current transport arrangement work?

☐ Yes
☐ Mostly
☐ Sometimes
☐ No
☐ It depends on where I’m going
What creates difficulty?
What currently works?
Safety & Emergency Access
This doesn’t need to become a giant risk assessment. We’re asking whether equipment or environmental factors affect the person’s ability to respond in an emergency.
Are there accessibility considerations someone should know about in an emergency?

☐ No
☐ Mobility
☐ Communication
☐ Hearing
☐ Vision
☐ Cognitive/executive functioning
☐ Panic/stress response
☐ Medication/health needs
☐ Equipment I rely on
☐ Assistance leaving my home
☐ Assistance contacting help
☐ Something else: __________
Is there anything important you would like recorded?
Equipment or Technology That Stops Working
Sometimes a person’s independence depends on equipment functioning.
If important equipment or technology stops working:

☐ I can manage temporarily without it
☐ I have a backup
☐ I know who to contact
☐ I need help organising repair/replacement
☐ I need additional assistance until it is restored
☐ I may be unable to complete particular everyday activities
☐ It can create a safety issue
☐ Something else: __________
☐ Not applicable
What happens for you?
Equipment Maintenance & Administration
Equipment can create work of its own.
Do you need to manage:

☐ Charging
☐ Cleaning
☐ Consumables
☐ Batteries
☐ Servicing
☐ Repairs
☐ Software/updates
☐ Replacement parts
☐ Appointments with suppliers
☐ Funding/approval paperwork
☐ Something else: __________
I manage this:

☐ Independently
☐ Using reminders/systems
☐ With occasional assistance
☐ With regular assistance
☐ Someone else manages most of it
☐ Not applicable
What support helps?
Things I Have Already Tried
You may already have tried equipment, technology or environmental changes that weren’t suitable.
Have you tried something that didn’t work?

☐ No
☐ Yes
☐ Partly
☐ I’m currently trialling something
What did you try?
What happened?
Why wasn’t it suitable?

☐ Didn’t meet my physical needs
☐ Too difficult to use
☐ Increased pain/fatigue
☐ Sensory difficulties
☐ Cognitive/executive demands
☐ Unreliable
☐ Didn’t fit my environment
☐ Required more assistance than expected
☐ Didn’t achieve what it was intended to achieve
☐ Something else: __________
Did you learn anything useful from trying it?
What Already Works
This is particularly important here because successful adaptations can make impairment less visible.
What equipment, technology or environmental adaptations currently work well for you?
What do they enable you to do?
What would be different without them?
That last question is important evidence.

Someone who can independently shower using an appropriate environmental adaptation isn’t evidence that they never had an accessibility need. It may be evidence that the adaptation is doing exactly what it was intended to do.
Do My Needs Change?

☐ My equipment/environment needs are fairly stable
☐ They change with fatigue
☐ They change with pain
☐ They change with physical health
☐ They change with mental/emotional health
☐ They change during flare-ups or deterioration
☐ My needs are gradually changing
☐ Something else: __________
On a better day, what can you manage?
On a more difficult day, what changes?
What Would Make My Environment Work Better for Me?
This is not automatically a request for funding.
It is an opportunity to identify barriers or adjustments that could make everyday life more accessible.
Is there anything that would help?

☐ Different equipment
☐ Adjustment to existing equipment
☐ Home modification/adaptation
☐ Different technology
☐ Communication technology
☐ Help learning or setting up technology
☐ Environmental/sensory adjustments
☐ Better physical accessibility
☐ Transport/access adjustment
☐ Professional assessment or advice
☐ I don’t currently need anything different
☐ I’m not sure
☐ Something else: __________
In your own words, what would make everyday life easier or more accessible?
What Difference Does the Right Environment Make?
When equipment, technology and the environment work for me:

☐ I can do more independently
☐ I need less physical assistance
☐ I use less energy
☐ I experience less pain/fatigue
☐ I feel safer
☐ I communicate more independently
☐ I can make more of my own choices
☐ I can leave home more easily
☐ I can access community environments
☐ I can maintain activities for longer
☐ I have more capacity for other parts of life
☐ I can participate in things that matter to me
☐ Something else: __________
What difference does it make for you?
In My Own Words
Sometimes changing the environment changes what is possible.
Equipment, technology and adaptations don’t define you. They may simply make it possible for you to use your abilities in ways that otherwise wouldn’t be accessible.
Is there anything about your equipment, technology, communication or environment that these questions haven’t captured?
You’ve completed this section
Update this section when there is a meaningful change in your equipment, technology, living environment or accessibility needs.
Your ongoing evidence can then show not only what you cannot do, but what becomes possible because an effective adjustment is already in place.

blocks.text: Module 14 — My Life, Purpose, Dreams & Aspirations
My life is more than the things I need help with

Throughout this Profile, you’ve been asked a lot about everyday life: what you can do, what is difficult, what takes extra effort, what support or adjustments you use, what already works and what helps you stay well.
Those things are important.
But they aren’t the whole of you.
People also have relationships, responsibilities, interests, roles, work, learning, beliefs, passions, contributions, enjoyment and things that give life meaning.
Some people have clear goals for the future.
Some are rebuilding parts of their life.
Some want to maintain the life they already have.
Some want more opportunities, connection, independence or purpose.
And some genuinely don’t know what they want next.
All of those are valid.
This section is about the life you are living now, what matters to you, what you don’t want to lose, and what—if anything—you would like more of in your life.
It is not a promise that every aspiration will be funded or provided by the NDIS.
It helps keep your everyday support and evidence connected to something much more important:
the life you actually want to live.
What Gives My Life Meaning?
Purpose doesn’t have to mean having a job, achieving something impressive or being busy.

It can come from relationships, caring for someone, raising children, animals, creativity, faith, work, learning, helping other people, belonging somewhere, maintaining your home, being part of a community—or simply living your life in a way that feels right to you.
Are there things that currently give you a sense of purpose or meaning?

☐ Family
☐ Partner/relationship
☐ Friendships
☐ Parenting
☐ Caring for or supporting someone
☐ Animals/pets
☐ Employment
☐ Running a business/self-employment
☐ Volunteering
☐ Study or learning
☐ Creative work
☐ Hobbies/interests
☐ Faith/spirituality
☐ Culture/community
☐ Helping other people
☐ Advocacy
☐ Looking after my home
☐ Physical activity/sport
☐ Being outdoors/nature
☐ Creating or building something
☐ Having responsibilities that matter to me
☐ Something else: __________
☐ I’m not sure what gives me purpose at the moment
☐ I’m currently trying to rediscover this
What gives your life meaning
to you
What makes you feel most like yourself?
The Roles I Have in My Life
A person isn’t only a participant, patient, client or recipient of support.
Roles that matter to me include:

☐ Parent
☐ Grandparent
☐ Partner
☐ Son/daughter
☐ Brother/sister
☐ Friend
☐ Carer
☐ Pet owner/carer
☐ Worker
☐ Employer/business owner
☐ Student
☐ Volunteer
☐ Community member
☐ Team/group member
☐ Mentor
☐ Creative person
☐ Someone other people rely on
☐ Another role: __________
Which roles are particularly important to you?
Does your disability or health affect your ability to participate in any of these roles?

☐ No
☐ Sometimes
☐ Yes
☐ It varies
What happens?
Is there support or an adjustment that helps you maintain those roles?
Employment & Work
Work can mean many things.
It might be paid employment, self-employment, casual work, running a business, working from home, supported employment or something else.
And not everybody needs or wants employment.
What describes you now?

☐ I work full-time
☐ I work part-time
☐ I work casually
☐ I’m self-employed
☐ I run a business
☐ I work from home
☐ I do supported employment
☐ I’m currently looking for work
☐ I’d like to work in the future
☐ I’m currently unable to work
☐ I’ve retired
☐ I don’t want paid employment
☐ I’m unsure what I want
☐ Something else: __________
If you currently work, what do you do?
What do you enjoy or value about it?
Does anything make working difficult?

☐ Physical demands
☐ Pain
☐ Fatigue
☐ Executive functioning
☐ Concentration
☐ Memory
☐ Communication
☐ Sensory environment
☐ Anxiety/panic
☐ Emotional or nervous-system demands
☐ Travel/transport
☐ Hours or scheduling
☐ Workplace accessibility
☐ Maintaining work alongside everyday living tasks
☐ Something else: __________
☐ Work isn’t significantly affected
What adjustments or support currently help?
If you’d like something different in relation to work, what would that be?
Education, Learning & Developing Skills
Learning doesn’t have an age limit and doesn’t have to mean formal education.
Are you currently:

☐ At school
☐ At university
☐ At TAFE/vocational training
☐ Completing another course
☐ Learning independently
☐ Learning practical/everyday skills
☐ Learning something simply because it interests me
☐ Not currently studying or learning anything formally
☐ Something else: __________
Is there something you enjoy learning about?
Is there something you’d like to learn?
Does anything make education or learning harder to access?

☐ Physical accessibility
☐ Fatigue
☐ Pain
☐ Concentration
☐ Executive functioning
☐ Memory
☐ Communication
☐ Sensory environment
☐ Anxiety
☐ Group environments
☐ Transport
☐ Technology
☐ How information is presented
☐ Something else: __________
☐ Nothing significant
What helps you learn?
Contribution & Volunteering
Purpose and contribution don’t have to involve paid work.
Do you currently contribute to something that matters to you?

☐ Volunteering
☐ Helping family
☐ Helping friends
☐ Caring for someone
☐ Community involvement
☐ Peer support
☐ Mentoring
☐ Advocacy
☐ Creative contribution
☐ Online/community participation
☐ Caring for animals
☐ Something else: __________
☐ Not currently
☐ I’d like to
What do you get from contributing?
Is there a way you would like to contribute that isn’t currently possible?
What gets in the way?
My Interests, Passions & Enjoyment
Not everything needs to have a productive purpose.
Enjoyment matters too.
Things I enjoy include:

☐ Music
☐ Art/creative activities
☐ Fashion/style/beauty
☐ Cooking/food
☐ Restaurants/cafés
☐ Sport
☐ Exercise/movement
☐ Gaming
☐ Technology
☐ Reading
☐ Movies/television
☐ Gardening
☐ Nature
☐ Animals
☐ Travel
☐ Going out
☐ Staying home
☐ Spending time with people
☐ Spending time alone
☐ Cultural activities
☐ Spiritual/faith activities
☐ Learning
☐ Making/building things
☐ Collecting things
☐ Something else: __________
What do you genuinely enjoy doing?
What do you look forward to?
Are you currently able to do the things you enjoy?

☐ Yes
☐ Mostly
☐ Sometimes
☐ Very little
☐ No
☐ I’m not sure what I enjoy anymore
If not, what gets in the way?
Things I Used to Do
Sometimes understanding what has been lost is important too.
Are there things you used to do that you no longer do?

☐ No
☐ Yes
☐ I’m not sure
What were they?
Why did they stop?

☐ Physical changes
☐ Health changes
☐ Pain
☐ Fatigue
☐ Mental health
☐ Executive functioning
☐ Anxiety/panic
☐ Accessibility
☐ Transport
☐ Loss of support
☐ Life circumstances changed
☐ People/relationships changed
☐ Financial circumstances
☐ I lost confidence
☐ I lost interest
☐ I don’t really know
☐ Something else: __________
Do you want any of those things back in your life?

☐ Yes
☐ Some of them
☐ No — that part of my life has finished
☐ I’m not sure
If yes, which ones matter to you?
That “No” option matters. We shouldn’t turn someone’s past into a rehabilitation target simply because they once did something.
What I Already Have & Don’t Want to Lose
This might be one of the most important parts of the final module.
A good life isn’t always about adding more.
Sometimes the goal is maintaining what is already precious.
What is already good in your life?
Are there things you have worked hard to establish that you want to maintain?
These might include:

☐ My home
☐ My independence
☐ Relationships
☐ Family contact
☐ Friendships
☐ My pet/animals
☐ Employment
☐ Study
☐ Volunteering
☐ Physical abilities
☐ Physical activity
☐ Health routines
☐ Community connection
☐ Hobbies/interests
☐ Emotional stability
☐ Daily routines
☐ Privacy
☐ Choice and control
☐ Something else: __________
Why are these important to you?
Does maintaining them require effort, adjustments or support that other people may not see?
Belonging & Connection
We covered connection as part of health in Module 10.
Here the question is slightly different:
Where do you feel you belong?
I feel a sense of belonging with:

☐ Family
☐ Friends
☐ Partner
☐ Neighbours
☐ Workplace
☐ School/study
☐ Cultural community
☐ Faith/spiritual community
☐ Disability/neurodivergent community
☐ Sporting/activity community
☐ Online community
☐ Local community
☐ Animals/pets
☐ A small number of individual people
☐ I don’t currently feel that I belong anywhere
☐ I’m comfortable without much community involvement
☐ Something else: __________
What does meaningful connection look like for you?
Would you like:

☐ More connection
☐ Less social demand
☐ Different kinds of connection
☐ More one-to-one connection
☐ More community involvement
☐ To maintain what I currently have
☐ I’m not sure
☐ Something else: __________
Choice, Independence & Control Over My Life
Independence doesn’t necessarily mean doing everything without help.
For some people, appropriate assistance is precisely what makes greater independence and choice possible.
What does independence mean
to you
Where do you currently feel you have good choice and control?
Are there areas where you would like more say over your own life?
Is there anything other people regularly assume you want that isn’t actually important to you?
I think that last question belongs in TMG.
What Would I Like More Of?
This doesn’t have to be a formal goal.
I would like more:

☐ Time with people I care about
☐ Meaningful connection
☐ Independence
☐ Choice/control
☐ Physical activity
☐ Time outside
☐ Enjoyment
☐ Rest
☐ Stability
☐ Purpose
☐ Work
☐ Learning
☐ Volunteering/contribution
☐ Creativity
☐ Community involvement
☐ Travel/adventure
☐ Confidence
☐ Privacy
☐ Time alone
☐ Opportunities to try things
☐ Something else: __________
☐ I’m content with this part of my life as it is
What would you like more of in your life?
What Would I Like Less Of?
Sometimes improving life means reducing something rather than adding another activity.
I would like less:

☐ Pain
☐ Fatigue
☐ Stress
☐ Overwhelm
☐ Administrative burden
☐ Having to explain myself repeatedly
☐ Isolation
☐ Unwanted social demands
☐ Dependence on other people
☐ Other people making decisions for me
☐ Time spent managing my health
☐ Time spent recovering
☐ Barriers to doing ordinary things
☐ Something else: __________
What would having less of this make possible?
Something I’d Like to Try
Is there anything you’ve thought:
“I’d like to do that one day”?
It can be large, small, practical, adventurous or seemingly ordinary.
Have you tried it before?

☐ Yes
☐ No
☐ Partly
☐ I used to do it
Is anything currently stopping you?
What might make it possible?
My Goals
You may already have formal NDIS goals, personal goals, health goals or goals that have nothing whatsoever to do with disability services.
Do you currently have goals that matter to you?
Are these:

☐ NDIS plan goals
☐ Personal goals
☐ Health goals
☐ Work goals
☐ Education goals
☐ Relationship/social goals
☐ Something else
☐ I don’t really think in terms of goals
Do your current formal goals still reflect what matters to you?

☐ Yes
☐ Mostly
☐ Some do
☐ No
☐ I’m not sure
☐ I don’t currently have formal goals
Is there anything you would change?
This matters because a person shouldn’t become permanently attached to a goal written during an assessment years earlier.
My Dreams & Aspirations
Now we can deliberately make the question bigger.
You don’t have to make your dreams realistic for an assessment.
You don’t have to know how they would happen.
And they don’t have to involve disability support.
Is there something you would really love to do, experience, become, create, learn or achieve?
Is there somewhere you’d love to go?
Is there something you’d love to learn?
Is there something you’d love to create or contribute?
Is there a relationship or connection you’d like more of?
Is there something you would like to regain?
Is there something you’ve never had the opportunity to try?
Or are you happy maintaining the life you have?

☐ Yes
☐ Mostly
☐ No
☐ I’m not sure
What Gets In The Way?
We have spent the previous modules identifying functional impacts in detail, so we don’t need to repeat the entire assessment here.
Instead:
Are there things you want in your life that are harder to access because of your disability, health or environment?

☐ No
☐ Yes
☐ Sometimes
☐ I’m not sure
What would you like to do?
What gets in the way?
Which earlier parts of your Profile help explain this?

☐ Body/movement
☐ Executive functioning
☐ Personal care
☐ Leaving home/getting around
☐ Food/nutrition
☐ Household functioning
☐ Mind/body health
☐ Emotions/nervous system
☐ Health/medication
☐ Equipment/environment
☐ Something else: __________
That’s where the architecture can eventually link domains rather than making the participant explain everything again.
What Would Appropriate Support Make Possible?
This is a better question than simply asking “What support do you want?”
If the barriers you’ve described were appropriately supported or adjusted, what would that allow you to do?
Would it help you:

☐ Maintain the life I already have
☐ Maintain my health or abilities
☐ Be more independent
☐ Have greater choice/control
☐ Work
☐ Study/learn
☐ Volunteer/contribute
☐ Maintain relationships
☐ Develop relationships
☐ Participate in my community
☐ Maintain hobbies/interests
☐ Return to something I’ve lost
☐ Try something new
☐ Have more capacity for ordinary everyday life
☐ Something else: __________
My Version of an Ordinary Good Life
And this is where I think the entire Profile should land.
Not on a clinical score.
Not on a funding request.
Not on an impairment.
Imagine your life working as well as it reasonably could for
you
It doesn’t have to look like anybody else’s life.
Where would you live?
Who would be part of your life?
How would you spend your days?
What would you do because you need to?
What would you do simply because you enjoy it?
What would give you purpose or meaning?
What would you like to be able to choose for yourself?
What would you want enough support with that it stopped consuming so much of your life?
What would you like to have enough energy, time or capacity left for?
In your own words, what does an ordinary good life mean to you?
Anything We Haven’t Asked?
A checklist can only ever suggest possibilities.
You are the person who knows your life.
Is there something important about you, your life, your purpose or your future that this Profile hasn’t asked?
Is there something you particularly want people supporting you to understand?
Is there anything you’ve written elsewhere in this Profile that you want to emphasise?
This Profile Belongs to You
This Profile describes your life at this point in time.

It can record what you do independently, what requires additional effort, what you need assistance with, what fluctuates, what already works, what helps maintain your health and abilities, and what matters to you beyond support.
You can update it when something meaningfully changes.
Your everyday records can add evidence over time without requiring you to continually retell your whole story.
And importantly:
You do not have to be constantly improving to have a meaningful life.
Maintaining abilities, relationships, health, independence, stability and things you already value can matter just as much as achieving something new.
Your aspirations are yours.
They don’t have to be impressive.
They don’t have to become NDIS goals.
And you don’t need to invent a new goal simply because somebody asks:
“What do you want to achieve?”
Sometimes the answer is:
“I want to keep the good things I already have.”
Sometimes it’s:
“There is something I really want to do.”
And sometimes it’s:
“I don’t know yet.”
All three tell us something important about who you truly are.
